title: Modeling Interference for Treatment Effect Estimation in Network Dynamic Environment
one_liner: Estimate treatment effects in changing networks by modeling both time-varying confounders and spillover from each person's treatment to neighbors' outcomes.
lead: Standard treatment-effect estimation assumes each person's treatment affects only that person's outcome. In a network this is often false. Vaccinating one person can protect nearby people. Showing one user an intervention can change what friends see or do. The problem becomes harder when the network and the confounders change over time. This paper defines a treatment effect that explicitly includes dynamic interference, then proposes DSPNET to estimate it from historical observations and network structure.

problem.h2: Why ordinary causal estimation fails on changing networks
paras: Treatment-effect estimation asks what would happen to an outcome if treatment were changed. Many methods assume each unit is isolated. In a network, that assumption breaks immediately because neighbors interact. One person's treatment can change another person's outcome through contact, information spread, or resource sharing.

Real networks also evolve. Links appear and disappear, and the variables that influence treatment and outcome change over time. If a method ignores that history, it can confuse spillover with direct treatment effect or miss the way past network states shaped who received treatment in the first place.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Define a treatment effect that includes dynamic neighbor spillover and estimate it with a history-aware network model, because direct and indirect effects are entangled when the graph changes over time.

steps.text: Specify a conditional treatment effect that allows a unit's outcome to depend on neighbor treatments in a dynamic graph, because spillover makes the isolated-unit target incomplete.
Summarize past covariates, treatments, outcomes, and network structure for each time step.
Use graph-aware message passing so neighbor treatments can influence the current estimate.
Use the historical summaries to control the factors that jointly affect treatment and outcome.
Estimate what the outcome would be under different own-treatment and neighbor-treatment histories.

paras: The paper changes the target of estimation itself. Instead of asking for a treatment effect under isolation, it asks for a treatment effect in which neighbor treatments and network history can also affect the outcome.
object.object: the estimand and estimator for treatment effect in a dynamic network

hidden.name: exposure history
paras: For each unit, the hidden quantity is not just 'treated or not treated.' It is the exposure history: the unit's own past treatments, neighbor treatments, and evolving network position.

This quantity matters because two units with the same current treatment can face very different causal pressure if one has many recently treated neighbors and the other has none. A method that ignores exposure history can mistake spillover for direct effect or mistake selection bias for treatment benefit.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark the historical exposure terms that must be tracked if interference is real.

reads.html: What matters is the full treatment neighborhood over time, not just whether one person was treated today.
CATE-ID depends on dynamic exposure history because both direct treatment and neighbor spillover influence the outcome process.

mechanism.h2: Why DSPNET can separate direct and spillover effects
paras: DSPNET uses history because treatment assignment and outcomes are both driven by evolving context. Past outcomes may influence future treatment, and past network structure may decide who interacts with whom next. Conditioning on that history helps the estimator avoid mixing cause with selection bias because it controls the variables that shaped both later treatment and later outcome.

The graph component matters because interference travels along links. If neighbor treatment changes your outcome, the estimator must read the local network state instead of treating every unit as independent. Message passing is useful here because it aggregates the current and past neighborhood information into each unit's representation.

The effect estimate becomes more credible when both pieces are present. Historical adjustment handles time-varying confounding, and graph-based aggregation handles spillover. Either piece alone leaves an identifiable gap in the causal story.

math.words: The target effect compares counterfactual outcomes under two treatment assignments while conditioning on a unit's observed history and network environment.
math.equation: CATE-ID = E[Y_t(a, n) - Y_t(a', n') | H_t]
symbols: the outcome at time t if the unit's own treatment were a and the neighbor exposure were n
the observed history up to time t

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a user can receive a recommendation today, and two close neighbors may also receive it.
Under own treatment on and neighbor exposure high, the predicted click probability is 0.42.
Under own treatment off and neighbor exposure low, the predicted click probability is 0.18.
The total contrast is 0.24, but DSPNET can also compare settings that change only own treatment or only neighbor exposure.
Those comparisons matter because they tell whether the gain came from direct treatment, spillover, or both.

math.note: The notation makes explicit that the outcome depends on both the unit's own treatment and the neighborhood treatment environment.

charts.title: Static no-interference estimator
charts.note: Ignoring dynamic spillover pushes several causal mechanisms into one crude estimate.

charts.title: Dynamic interference estimator
charts.note: The graph-and-history model helps because it conditions on the factors that actually drive dynamic exposure.

items.html: If an important time-varying driver of treatment and outcome is never observed, no estimator can fully remove that bias. DSPNET still depends on the identifiability assumptions being at least approximately true.

items.b: Observed links may miss real influence paths.
items.html: A recorded social graph is often incomplete. Missing links matter because spillover can travel along unseen connections that the model never gets to use.

The method needs enough longitudinal data to distinguish direct treatment, spillover, and confounding. Short or sparse records make those signals hard to separate because several explanations fit the same few observations.
The method is most persuasive when the application truly has changing links and plausible spillover, because those are the cases where static isolated-unit assumptions are least defensible.

paras: Simulate a small dynamic contact network in which treatment can affect both the treated node and its neighbors. Let treatment assignment depend on past outcomes so time-varying confounding is real. Compare a static isolated-unit estimator against DSPNET on recovery of direct effect and spillover effect. The paper's point is visible if DSPNET recovers both parts with lower bias because it models history and neighbor exposure together.
demo.closing: The demo should include a case with no interference and a case with strong interference, because that shows exactly when the extra graph machinery becomes necessary.
